I have farmed these 11.6 mu in Quzhou for fifty years, and I know every corner of this land. My father taught me the cotton-wheat relay system, and I still use it on 5 mu because it gives us wheat grain in early June while the cotton keeps growing through to autumn harvest—that is two crops from one piece of ground, and the cotton income pays for the children's expenses. On the remaining land, I plant 3 mu of maize for animal feed and some cash, 2 mu of millet because it does not drink much water from my well, and 1.6 mu of mungbean because as a legume it asks for almost no nitrogen and the green pods fetch a good price in summer. I am sixty-five now, so I rely on what has proven itself: improved wheat and cotton seeds that I have saved from last year, hybrid maize because the yield jump is too big to ignore, and rotary tillage for everything except cotton, which needs deep ploughing to break the hard pan after years of monoculture. I will irrigate cotton four times and wheat three times because they are the thirstiest; maize twice; millet and mungbean only once each since the summer rains usually help them. Cotton gets the most fertilizer because it is a heavy feeder and my biggest cash earner, while mungbean gets barely any nitrogen since it fixes its own. I spray pesticides most often on cotton—seven times—to keep bollworms away, and only once or twice on the other crops because I cannot afford to let pests take everything, but I also do not want to waste money on chemicals where they are not needed.
